## The ticket

Monday, 7:50 a.m. Your Quality Analyst is standing in your doorway before you've finished your
coffee, holding a printout with one line highlighted in yellow.

Friday night, Lakeshore ran a scheduled overnight maintenance window on BECS (Blood
Establishment Computer Software — the system that gates donor eligibility, quarantine release,
and labeling across every collection site). During the window, Lakeshore's Brookfield satellite
collection site — open Friday evenings, without a live BECS connection during downtime — switched
to its paper downtime procedure, the way it's supposed to. Staff checked each donor against the
site's printed deferred-donor list from the downtime binder, the way they're supposed to.

One donor, Owen Pruitt, had been deferred two days earlier — Tuesday — at Lakeshore's downtown
donor center, after disclosing recent travel to a country on the malaria-risk list during his
history interview. The Brookfield site's printed list was dated the previous Monday. Owen's
deferral wasn't on it. He donated Friday night. Nobody at Brookfield did anything wrong by the
binder they had in front of them.

This morning's post-downtime reconciliation — entering Friday night's paper transactions into
BECS — hit his donor ID and BECS immediately flagged him: deferred, active, reason on file. Your
QA already checked what happened to the unit. A leukoreduced red cell component from that
donation cleared testing Saturday, released from quarantine Sunday, and shipped to Riverside
General Hospital to fill a standing order. It's sitting in Riverside's inventory right now,
untransfused, as far as anyone knows.

"I need to open a deviation," she says. "I don't know yet how much further this goes."

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

This is QSE 7 in AABB's Quality System Essentials framework — **Deviations, Nonconformances, and
Adverse Events** — the drawer module 1 told you to come back to when a real event landed on your
desk. This is that event, opened up in full.

Start with the failure mode this QSE exists to prevent: an organization that only *reacts* to
things going wrong, inconsistently, with no record of what it did or why, learns nothing and
proves nothing. A deviation system exists to force the same four questions every time, regardless
of how minor the event looks in the moment: what happened, how far did it spread, what did we do
about the product, and does anyone outside this building need to know. Skip it and you get exactly
what almost happened here: a donor whose donation should have been blocked, caught not by a
control built to catch it, but by routine data entry three days later — after a unit had already
left the building.

You already run this triage constantly. When something breaks, you open an incident, you
diagnose and contain it, you restore service, you close the ticket. A deviation write-up is
*structurally* an incident record — same discovery-to-closure shape, same instinct to contain
first and ask why later. But the quality version demands three things ITIL incident management
was never built to ask:

- **Product disposition.** Your "service" here is a physical unit of blood sitting in a hospital
  refrigerator. Closing an IT incident means service is restored. Closing this one means someone
  with the authority to decide has determined, in writing, what happens to that physical unit —
  and to every other unit that might be connected to it.
- **A regulatory clock that starts at discovery, not at resolution.** The `risk-and-controls-
  vocabulary` foundation already walked you through 606.171's 45-day reporting clock. It starts
  the moment you have information suggesting a reportable event — this morning, for Lakeshore —
  whether or not the investigation is finished.
- **Impact assessment as extent-of-condition, not "which users are affected."** An incident asks
  who's degraded right now. A deviation asks a colder question: what *else* does this touch — other
  units from the same donation, other donors checked against the same stale list, other sites
  still running the same downtime binder.

`becs-in-the-pipeline` called this "one incident, two tracks" — an IT incident track that closes
when service is restored, and a separate quality/deviation track that closes only when Quality has
documented its determination. This module *is* that second track, run start to finish.

## Vocabulary check: four words that get used loosely

AABB's framework — and most real quality systems — use these terms without drawing hard lines
between them, and that's worth saying plainly rather than pretending otherwise. What actually
matters to an assessor isn't which word Lakeshore's SOP picks; it's that the SOP defines its terms
and applies them consistently.

- **Deviation** — a departure from an approved policy, process, procedure, regulation, or
  specification. Brookfield collecting from a deferred donor is a deviation from 630.10(h) below.
- **Nonconformance** — a failure to meet a specified requirement, often used for a product or
  material that doesn't meet spec. Overlaps heavily with "deviation" in everyday use.
- **Adverse event** — an untoward occurrence tied to a donor or a patient. Not what happened here —
  no one was harmed — but it's the third word in this QSE's name because the same intake-and-
  investigate machinery handles all three.
- **Near-miss** — an event caught before its potential consequence materialized, with no product
  affected. The foundation's label-swap example was a near-miss. This one isn't — a component
  shipped — which is why the analysis below lands harder than it would have if reconciliation had
  caught it Saturday morning instead of Monday.
- **Complaint** — a problem reported from outside Lakeshore (a hospital, a donor) instead of found
  internally. Not this event, but a fifth entry point into the same process.

## The process in plain English

Five stages, and Owen Pruitt's donation runs through all five.

**1. Discovery.** However it's found — routine reconciliation, an audit, a complaint, a monitoring
alarm, self-report — the clock (both the internal investigation clock and, potentially, 606.171's
45-day clock) starts here, at the moment of discovery, not when the deviation record gets opened
or the investigation wraps up. For Lakeshore, discovery was Monday morning's reconciliation entry.

**2. Immediate containment and correction.** Before anything else: stop the bleeding. This is
*correction* in the foundation's sense — fixing this instance, not the process. For this event,
containment means: quarantine any remaining component from Owen's donation still in Lakeshore's
inventory immediately, and notify Riverside General Hospital, today, that the shipped unit needs
to be held and not transfused pending Lakeshore's determination. Containment doesn't wait for the
investigation to finish, and it doesn't require knowing yet whether the event is reportable.

**3. Impact and extent assessment.** Now ask the colder question: what else does this touch?
Apply the likelihood/severity/detectability reasoning the foundation already gave you — don't
re-derive it, just run it. Severity here is real: a donor deferred specifically for
travel-related transfusion-transmitted-infection risk actually donated, and the unit reached a
hospital. Detectability was poor: nothing in the downtime process itself caught it; only
unrelated, routine data entry three days later did. Extent-of-condition means checking further
than this one unit: were other components prepared from Owen's donation, and where are they now?
Did any *other* donor get checked against that same stale list during Friday's downtime window? Is
the binder's superseded list-refresh procedure running at any other satellite site right now?
That last question is the one that turns "one donor's donation" into "how many sites have this
exposure."

**4. Product disposition.** Someone with documented disposition authority — whoever Lakeshore's
SOP names for this, typically the medical director or a delegated quality officer, not whoever
happens to be on shift — decides, in writing, what happens to the product: quarantine, destroy,
retrieve, or release. For Owen's unit, disposition is straightforward once containment has already
put a hold on it at Riverside: it stays quarantined pending Lakeshore's full determination and does
not get transfused. The disposition record proves that decision was made deliberately, by someone
with the authority to make it — not that the unit happened to still be sitting in a fridge when
someone thought to check.

**5. Documented reportability determination.** This is 606.171, already taught in full in the
foundation — apply it, don't re-derive it. Run the test: does this event represent a deviation
from an applicable regulation that may affect safety, purity, or potency (606.171(b)(1)(i)), and
does it involve *distributed* product (606.171(b)(3))? Here, both are true, and this isn't a close
call. Collecting from a donor deferred under 630.10(h) is a direct deviation from an applicable
regulation; the deferral reason exists specifically because travel to certain regions carries a
transfusion-transmitted-infection risk, which is exactly the kind of thing that "may affect"
safety; and the red cell unit was released and shipped to Riverside. This is reportable. Say so
plainly rather than softening it — a documented "not reportable" would be the wrong conclusion on
these facts. The 45-day clock started Monday, at discovery, not whenever the write-up gets
finished. (Filing Form FDA-3486 itself — the BPDR's filing mechanics — belongs to a later course;
this module stops at the determination.)

Then the sixth question, which decides where this event goes next.

**Does this need a CAPA (corrective and preventive action — the process that fixes not just this
instance, but the system that allowed it)?** The line isn't drawn by the form; it's drawn by the
question you're asking. "What happened, to what, how far did it spread, and what did we do with
the product" is deviation management — everything above. "Why did the system let this happen, and
how do we prove it won't recur" is a different question entirely, and it's CAPA's whole job. In
practice, plenty of organizations put a short cause statement right on the deviation form, and a
small event might get nothing more than that. But this one doesn't stay small once you look at it:
the proximate explanation is "Brookfield's downtime binder held a superseded SOP revision that
didn't require refreshing the deferred-donor list immediately before a downtime event." That's not
"staff used the wrong binder" — staff followed the binder they had, correctly. It's a document-
control gap that could be sitting at every other satellite site right now, which means "retrain the
Brookfield staff" would fix nothing. **Yes, this needs a CAPA**, with that proximate cause as its
starting point — and *why* that's the right call, not "human error," is the next module's entire
job.

One more thing worth stating explicitly, because it's a genuinely common point of confusion: the
deviation and the CAPA run on **different clocks**. Lakeshore can close this deviation record —
disposition made, reportability determined and filed — without waiting for the CAPA to finish
investigating and fixing the underlying document-control gap. Closing the deviation says "we know
what happened to this product and we've told the people we're required to tell." Closing the CAPA,
much later, says "we've proven the system won't do this again." Don't let a deviation sit open for
weeks waiting on a CAPA that hasn't even started its root-cause work.

A one-line note on a related but different animal: a **planned deviation** (a pre-approved
exception to a policy, justified and signed off *before* it happens, typically requiring the
medical director's approval) is the controlled cousin of what just happened at Brookfield — this
one wasn't planned or approved by anyone, which is exactly what makes it reportable instead of
routine. Planned deviations get their real treatment in the change-control module later in this
course.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(b) | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph b" | Written SOPs required for, among other things, "all steps in the investigation of product deviations related to § 606.171," available to staff in the areas where they're performed. | The regulatory floor under Lakeshore's whole deviation-investigation process — and under the downtime binder itself, which is a procedure that has to be current where it's used. |
| 21 CFR 630.10(e)(2)(iii) | "Six-thirty point one-oh, paragraph e, sub-two, clause iii" | Travel to, or residence in, an area endemic for a transfusion-transmitted infection is an eligibility factor the donor history assessment must cover. | The basis for Owen's Tuesday deferral at the downtown center. |
| 21 CFR 630.10(h) | "Six-thirty point one-oh, paragraph h" | An establishment must not collect from a donor found ineligible or deferred, unless an exception applies. | The specific rule Brookfield's stale list caused Lakeshore to violate Friday night — the deviation at the center of this event. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(b)(1)(i) / (b)(3) | "Six-oh-six point one-seven-one, paragraph b, sub-one, clause i / sub-three" | A deviation from an applicable regulation that may affect safety, purity, or potency, involving *distributed* product, is reportable. | Already taught in full in `risk-and-controls-vocabulary`. Applied here: both prongs are met, so this event is reportable. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(b)(7)(iii) | "Six-oh-six point one-sixty, paragraph b, sub-seven, clause iii" | Biological product deviations must be kept among an establishment's general records. | The record that has to exist once the 606.171 determination is made — the deviation record itself, filed and retrievable. |

## The actual text

The SOP requirement behind the whole investigation process, quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/606.100.md` — the clause naming product-deviation investigations specifically, not
quoted by any earlier lesson in this curriculum:

> Establishments must establish, maintain, and follow written standard operating procedures for
> all steps in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage, and distribution of
> blood and blood components for allogeneic transfusion, autologous transfusion, and further
> manufacturing purposes; for all steps in the investigation of product deviations related to
> § 606.171; and for all steps in recordkeeping related to current good manufacturing practice and
> other applicable requirements and standards. Such procedures must be available to the personnel
> for use in the areas where the procedures are performed.

Read the last sentence with Brookfield specifically in mind: "available to the personnel for use
in the areas where the procedures are performed" is the regulation's own language for exactly the
gap this event exposes — a downtime binder physically present at the satellite site, but holding a
superseded revision. Available and current aren't the same thing, and this sentence expects both.

The eligibility rule Friday's donation violated, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/630.10.md`:

> (h) *What must you do when a donor is not eligible?* You must not collect blood or blood
> components from a donor found to be ineligible prior to collection based on criteria in
> §§ 630.10 or 630.15, or deferred under § 610.41 of this chapter or § 630.30(b)(2), unless this
> subchapter provides an exception. You must defer donors found to be ineligible and you must
> notify the donor of their deferral under § 630.40.

No exception in this subchapter covers "the site's copy of the deferral list was several days
old." That's precisely why this is a deviation and not a judgment call.

606.100(c)'s investigation standard, already quoted in full in the foundation — worth its last
sentence here, since it's the clause that requires the write-up itself, not just the disposition:

> A thorough investigation, including the conclusions and followup, of any unexplained discrepancy
> or the failure of a lot or unit to meet any of its specifications shall be made and recorded.

And the record requirement that closes the loop, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.160.md`:

> (7) General records: ... (iii) Biological product deviations.

A reportability determination that only lives in an email thread doesn't satisfy this. It has to
land in the general records this clause names.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor pulling this deviation file wants four things, and a gap in
any one is a finding on its own — regardless of whether the underlying event ever caused harm.

**A timestamped discovery date**, tied to when Lakeshore actually acquired the information — the
Monday reconciliation entry, not the Friday donation. This is what the 45-day clock measures
against, and a vague or backdated discovery date turns a defensible reportability call into a
credibility problem fast.

**Evidence that containment happened before the investigation finished.** Riverside's hold
notification and the quarantine of any remaining product need timestamps that land the same day as
discovery, not "eventually," once the full write-up was complete.

**A documented extent-of-condition check**, not "checked, nothing else found." What sites were
reviewed, what was searched for, and what the negative result actually rules out. "We looked" is
not an artifact; a list of what was checked is.

**The reportability determination itself, in writing, with the reasoning shown** — even when the
answer would have been "not reportable." A file that jumps from "here's what happened" straight to
"here's the CAPA," with no visible 606.171 analysis in between, reads as an avoided question.

## Common traps

**"We contained it, so the deviation is closed."** Containment stops the immediate problem —
Riverside holding the unit — but it doesn't answer any of the other four questions this process
demands: how far it spread, what the formal disposition is, whether it's reportable, and whether
it needs a CAPA. A deviation record that stops at "contained" the same day is missing most of its
own required content.

**"Every deviation needs a CAPA" — or its mirror image, "this one clearly doesn't need one."** Both
are wrong the same way: they skip the reasoning. Some deviations genuinely close with a short cause
statement and no formal CAPA — a legitimate outcome, not a shortcut, *as long as the reasoning is
written down.* What an inspector penalizes isn't "too few" or "too many" CAPAs — it's a CAPA
decision, in either direction, with no documented rationale behind it.

**Confusing the correction with the deviation record.** Holding Owen's unit at Riverside is a
correction — necessary, immediate, and not itself the deviation record. The deviation record is
the document that captures discovery, containment, impact assessment, disposition, reportability,
and the CAPA decision, together, as one traceable file. Treating the correction as if it *were* the
record — "we fixed it, so we're done documenting" — is how a file ends up with a quarantine
timestamp and nothing else.

## What this means for your job

- **When your QA hands you a deviation, ask for all five pieces in writing, every time:**
  discovery date, containment, extent-of-condition, disposition, and the 606.171 call. A file
  missing any one of the five isn't finished, regardless of how the event turned out.
- **Treat "caught before it caused harm" and "handled" as two different claims.** This event's
  severity didn't change because reconciliation eventually caught it; it changed because a unit
  had already shipped by the time anyone looked.
- **Push back on a CAPA decision — yes or no — that doesn't show its reasoning.** "Low risk,
  closed" and "opened a CAPA" are both fine answers. Neither is acceptable without the
  likelihood/severity/detectability reasoning behind it.
- **Ask whether the extent-of-condition check reached other sites, not just other units from this
  one donation.** The real exposure isn't Owen's unit — it's every satellite site that might be
  running the same superseded downtime binder right now.
- **Watch the two clocks separately.** Don't let a deviation sit open waiting on CAPA progress,
  and don't let a CAPA get rushed because someone wants the deviation file closed by month-end.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA says, "The red cell unit hasn't been transfused yet, so this isn't reportable — nothing was actually affected." Accurate?

No. 606.171(b)(1)'s test is "may affect," not "did affect," and paragraph (b)(3)'s trigger is
*distribution*, not transfusion. The unit left Lakeshore's control and reached Riverside — that
satisfies (b)(3) on its own. Whether it was ever transfused is a fact worth knowing for the
investigation, but it doesn't change whether the reporting trigger was met. This is the exact
"caught in time" mistake the foundation's label-mix-up example was built to head off, now showing
up with a real distributed unit instead of a near-miss.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Does every deviation at Lakeshore need a full CAPA?

No — and that's not a loophole, it's the honest answer. The deviation-versus-CAPA line is drawn by
the question being asked, not by a rule that every open deviation escalates automatically. A small,
well-understood, one-off event can close with a short cause statement and no formal CAPA, and that
can be entirely correct. What makes this particular event different is the proximate cause: a
superseded procedure surviving in active use at a remote site isn't a one-off human mistake, it's
a systemic gap that's plausibly sitting at other sites too — which is exactly the kind of finding
that has to become a CAPA. The requirement isn't "open a CAPA for everything." It's "write down why
you did or didn't," every time, so the decision can survive someone else reading the file later.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Your QA argues, "We don't need to check whether any other Brookfield donors were affected Friday night — Owen's the only one who was actually deferred." Reasonable?

No. Extent-of-condition assessment isn't about who was deferred — it's about who was checked
against a control that was broken at the time. Every donor screened at Brookfield during Friday's
downtime window was checked against the same stale list, which means the same failure mode was
live for all of them, whether or not any of them happened to be deferred. The investigation has to
show that check was actually run, with a stated result, not just assume it because only one match
turned up. This is also where the question about *other sites* running the same superseded binder
revision belongs — the same reasoning, one level up.
:::

## Where this goes next

The deviation record is closable: discovery, containment, impact assessment, disposition, and a
documented "yes, this is reportable" determination are all in place. What's still open is the
harder question this module deliberately didn't answer — not "what happened," but "why did the
system let it happen, and how do we prove the fix actually works." That's `capa-root-cause-to-
effectiveness`, the next module, and it picks up this exact event: the same superseded downtime
binder, the same stale deferral list, starting from the CAPA decision this module just made.
